paragraphs.source_en: A year and two months had passed since Ieyasu had been appointed Seii Taishōgun. The realm had been settled during that time, yet the ever-cautious Ieyasu did not relax his vigilance on that account. He understood that what he saw and heard in Edo was no reliable measure of whether the realm he had built with his own hands truly had the people's support and accorded with their wishes; that could be seen clearly only outside Edo.

paragraphs.source_en: Kyushu was a place of military importance, and it was therefore essential to work in concert with the Shimazu clan. As soon as Ieyasu reached Fushimi, he summoned Shimazu Tadatsune, who had just arrived in the capital, and first selected a site for a Shimazu residence at Kinoshita in Kyoto. Both the Shimazu and the Mōri had fought against Ieyasu at the Battle of Sekigahara. But now that they had sworn loyalty to Ieyasu's new government, he did not cling to old grievances; instead, he displayed the full breadth of his magnanimity and set their minds at ease.

paragraphs.source_en: Another purpose of Ieyasu's journey to the capital was to learn what the imperial court and the court nobles thought of the new government. The court nobles were acutely sensitive to affairs of state and public sentiment. Having survived beside the imperial family for a thousand years, they possessed an extraordinarily keen instinct for the rise and fall of the realm and for order and disorder in the age. They were sure to have opinions of their own about what Ieyasu had done over the past year.

paragraphs.source_en: Accordingly, on the twenty-second day of the sixth month Ieyasu entered the palace for an audience with the emperor, and on the twenty-third he went to Nijō Castle, where he awaited those coming to pay their respects. Their response surprised Ieyasu somewhat. Those who came to see him included not only court nobles, but imperial princes and the abbots of imperial temples as well. As it was their first meeting with Ieyasu that year, they offered their congratulations with the utmost respect. It was plain that they felt more secure than they had under Toyotomi Hideyoshi's rule.

paragraphs.source_en: That very day, Ieyasu ordered warriors from seven regions, including Ise, Mino, and Owari, to assist Ii Naokatsu in building the new Hikone Castle at Sawayama, formerly the seat of Ishida Mitsunari. The Ii clan had been renowned since the Northern and Southern Courts for its loyalty to the emperor. Entrusting the defense of the imperial capital to the Ii and thereby making Kyoto impregnable was at once a show of strength and a reassurance.

paragraphs.source_en: Not long afterward, Ieyasu received three pieces of good news in succession. A messenger from Ōkubo Nagayasu reported that he had unearthed a great quantity of gold on Sado. Ieyasu had not demanded it, but the act was immensely significant, for it showed that the military lords too were beginning to understand his new government.
